title: Climate change
summary: The human causes of climate change, positive feedbacks and tipping points, impacts on polar, ocean, mountain and coral reef ecosystems, carbon sequestration, and effects on the timing of biological events and evolution.

keyterms.definition: Increased warming of the Earth caused by rising atmospheric concentrations of greenhouse gases from human activities.
Caused by human activity, e.g. CO2 from burning fossil fuels and methane from livestock and landfill.
A process in which warming causes changes that cause further warming, accelerating climate change.
Proportion of incoming solar radiation reflected by a surface; high for ice and snow, low for ocean and forest.
Ground that stays frozen all year; contains large stores of organic matter that release CO2 and methane when thawed.
Threshold beyond which boreal forest switches from net carbon accumulation to net carbon loss.
Sea ice attached to the coast or sea floor; used as a stable breeding habitat, e.g. by emperor penguins.
Rising of cold, nutrient-rich deep water to the ocean surface, supporting high phytoplankton productivity.
Movement of a species' distribution, typically poleward or upslope, as temperatures rise.
Loss of mutualistic zooxanthellae from coral tissues when water is too warm, leaving the coral white and short of food.
Fall in ocean pH as dissolved CO2 forms carbonic acid, reducing carbonate ions available for skeletons and shells.
Long-term capture and storage of atmospheric carbon, e.g. by afforestation, forest regeneration and restoring peat-forming wetlands.
Study of the timing of seasonal biological events, such as flowering, migration and breeding, and their cues.
Loss of synchrony between interacting species' life events because they respond to different cues, e.g. photoperiod versus temperature.
Two or more distinct heritable forms (morphs) of a species within one population, e.g. grey and brown tawny owls.

questions.prompt: What is the main anthropogenic cause of the recent rise in atmospheric CO2?
options: Respiration by a growing human population
Volcanic eruptions
Combustion of fossil fuels
Photosynthesis by crops
questions.explanation: Burning coal, oil and gas releases carbon that was locked away for millions of years. Deforestation adds to this; human respiration is part of the short-term carbon cycle.

questions.statement: The greenhouse effect itself is natural and keeps Earth warm enough for life; climate change results from the enhanced greenhouse effect.
questions.explanation: Greenhouse gases always trapped some long-wave radiation. Human emissions have increased their concentrations, trapping more heat.

questions.prompt: Match each source to the greenhouse gas it mainly releases.

pairs.right: Carbon dioxide from combustion of biomass

questions.explanation: CO2 comes mostly from combustion; methane is produced by methanogenic archaea in anaerobic conditions such as rumens, paddies and landfill.

questions.prompt: Order this positive feedback loop involving ice.
items: Darker land and ocean are exposed, lowering albedo
questions.explanation: Ice reflects most sunlight; once it is replaced by darker surfaces, more energy is absorbed, amplifying the original warming.

questions.text: Thawing ___ allows decomposition of stored organic matter, releasing CO2 and methane.
questions.explanation: Frozen soils hold huge carbon stores because decomposition is very slow. Warming speeds decomposition, releasing greenhouse gases — a positive feedback.

questions.prompt: Why is warming of the oceans a positive feedback for climate change?
options: Warm water holds more dissolved CO2
Warmer water holds less dissolved CO2, so CO2 is released to the atmosphere
Warm water reflects more sunlight
Warm water increases phytoplankton photosynthesis everywhere
questions.explanation: Gas solubility decreases with temperature. Oceans absorb less CO2 and may release some, increasing atmospheric CO2 and further warming.

questions.prompt: How could boreal forests reach a tipping point?
options: Higher CO2 makes trees grow faster indefinitely
Snowfall increases, protecting trees
Cooler summers reduce photosynthesis
Drought, fires and insect pest outbreaks kill trees, so carbon released exceeds carbon absorbed
questions.explanation: When losses from fire, decomposition and respiration exceed uptake by photosynthesis, the forest changes from a carbon sink to a carbon source, adding to warming.

questions.statement: Increased droughts and forest fires caused by warming are an example of a negative feedback that slows climate change.
questions.explanation: Fires release CO2 and reduce photosynthesis, which increases atmospheric CO2 and causes further warming — a positive feedback.

questions.text: Fresh snow and ice have a high ___, reflecting most incoming sunlight.
questions.explanation: High-albedo surfaces reflect solar radiation back to space, so their loss increases absorption of energy.

questions.prompt: Which is a correct example of a tipping point?
options: A system that returns to its original state after a small disturbance
A threshold beyond which a system shifts rapidly to a new state that is hard to reverse
A gradual, linear change that stops when the cause is removed
A seasonal fluctuation in temperature
questions.explanation: Tipping points involve self-reinforcing changes (positive feedback). Once passed, removing the original cause may not restore the original state.

lessons.title: Impacts on ecosystems and carbon sequestration

questions.prompt: Why does loss of landfast ice threaten emperor penguins?
options: They breed on stable landfast ice, which may break up before chicks are ready to swim
They feed only on the ice surface
Landfast ice provides their drinking water
Melting ice raises sea levels over their nests on land
questions.explanation: Emperor penguins need ice that remains attached to the coast for the whole breeding season. Early break-up drowns or exposes chicks that have not yet fledged.

questions.statement: Loss of sea ice forces walruses to haul out on land in crowded groups, far from their feeding grounds.
questions.explanation: Walruses rest on sea ice above shallow feeding areas. Without it, they gather on beaches where stampedes kill young and they must travel further to feed.

questions.text: Cold, nutrient-rich deep water rising to the surface is called ___.
questions.explanation: Upwelling supplies nitrates and phosphates to phytoplankton, supporting productive fisheries. Changes in currents alter its timing and extent.

questions.prompt: Why does surface ocean warming tend to reduce nutrient supply to phytoplankton?
options: Warm water contains more nutrients
Phytoplankton cannot photosynthesize in warm water
Warm surface water is less dense, increasing stratification and reducing mixing with nutrient-rich deep water
Warming increases upwelling
questions.explanation: Stronger layering acts as a barrier to vertical mixing, so fewer nutrients reach the sunlit zone, lowering productivity and affecting food chains.

questions.prompt: Match each climate change impact to its example.

pairs.right: Temperate species moving poleward and upslope
Melting sea ice used by walruses
Corals expel zooxanthellae in warm water
Change in timing of nutrient supply to plankton

questions.explanation: Climate change affects species distributions, habitats and ecosystem processes.

questions.statement: Species living near mountain summits are especially at risk from upslope range shifts.
questions.explanation: As temperatures rise, suitable conditions move higher. Species already at the top have nowhere colder to move, so their habitat shrinks and may disappear.

questions.prompt: Order the events in ocean acidification affecting corals.
items: Carbonic acid forms and pH falls
Corals deposit calcium carbonate skeletons more slowly
questions.explanation: Fewer carbonate ions make it harder for corals and other marine calcifiers to build calcium carbonate structures.

questions.prompt: Why can coral bleaching lead to ecosystem collapse?
options: Bleached coral is poisonous to fish
Corals lose the photosynthetic algae that supply most of their food, and if this persists the corals die, removing habitat for many species
Bleaching causes corals to grow too fast
Bleaching increases ocean pH
questions.explanation: Reef-building corals provide the physical structure of the reef. Their death, combined with acidification, threatens the many species that depend on reefs.

questions.text: Planting trees on land that has not recently been forested is called ___.
questions.explanation: Afforestation and forest regeneration remove CO2 by photosynthesis and store carbon in biomass and soil.

questions.prompt: Why does restoring peat-forming wetlands sequester carbon?
options: Waterlogged, acidic, anaerobic conditions slow decomposition, so dead plant matter accumulates as peat
Wetlands release methane, cooling the climate
Peat is burned to release energy
Wetland plants do not respire
questions.explanation: Saprotrophs are inhibited in waterlogged acidic conditions, so organic carbon is stored rather than respired. Drained peatlands, by contrast, release CO2.

questions.prompt: Which two environmental cues commonly control the timing of phenological events?
options: Photoperiod and temperature
Rainfall and wind direction
Soil pH and salinity
Lunar cycle and humidity only
questions.explanation: Many organisms time flowering, migration or breeding using day length and/or temperature.

questions.statement: Climate change alters photoperiod as well as temperature.
questions.explanation: Day length depends on latitude and date, so it is unchanged. Temperature cues shift, so species relying on temperature change their timing while those relying on photoperiod do not.

questions.prompt: In Greenland, caribou calving is timed by photoperiod while plant growth is triggered by temperature. What is the consequence of warming?
options: Calving shifts earlier to match plant growth
Plants grow later, after calving
Plant growth peaks earlier, so calves are born after peak food availability
There is no effect on calf survival
questions.explanation: Plants respond to warming by growing earlier but calving does not shift, causing a phenological mismatch that reduces food for lactating females and calves.

questions.text: Loss of synchrony between a predator's breeding and its prey's peak abundance is called phenological ___.
questions.explanation: For example, if winter moth caterpillars peak earlier with warmer springs but great tits do not lay earlier, nestlings miss the food peak.

questions.prompt: How has climate change affected spruce bark beetles in Alaska?
options: Cold winters have killed most beetles
Warmer temperatures allow them to complete their life cycle in one year instead of two, increasing outbreaks
They have stopped feeding on spruce
They now only reproduce asexually
questions.explanation: More generations per unit time means faster population growth. Large outbreaks have killed millions of spruce trees, adding to boreal forest carbon loss.

questions.prompt: Match each example to the climate change effect it shows.

pairs.right: More insect life cycles within a year
Evolution due to changing selection pressure

questions.explanation: Climate change affects the timing of events, the speed of life cycles, and the direction of natural selection.

questions.prompt: In Finland, the proportion of brown tawny owls has increased relative to grey ones. What explains this?
options: Owls change colour in their lifetime to match the environment
Brown owls migrated from the south
Grey owls were hunted by humans
With less snow cover, grey owls lose their camouflage and survival advantage, so brown morph alleles increase
questions.explanation: Colour is heritable. Milder winters with less snow reduced selection for grey owls and favoured brown ones, changing allele frequencies — evolution driven by climate change.

questions.statement: The tawny owl example shows evolution because the frequency of a heritable trait changed in the population over generations.
questions.explanation: Individual owls do not change colour; differential survival of the heritable morphs changed the population's composition.

questions.prompt: Order the sequence leading to mismatch between great tits and caterpillars.
items: Oak leaves and winter moth caterpillars appear earlier
Nestlings hatch after the caterpillar peak
questions.explanation: When species respond to warming at different rates, consumers miss the peak of their food supply.

questions.text: The study of the timing of seasonal biological events is called ___.
questions.explanation: Phenology records, for example, first flowering dates, bird arrival dates and insect emergence, often over many decades.
